headline: Utah has opened three new health care pilots in which AI refills prescriptions, writes first acne prescriptions and gives physical therapy, while its own regulator admits that liability and FDA oversight are still unsettled.
score_reason: Pool 7, lowered to 6: the pilots were announced last week and the remarks date from 15 Oct, before the 16 Oct window; no results from the pilots yet.
importance_line: Utah patients may get routine prescriptions and physical therapy from AI under state supervision, doctors and regulators have not settled who is liable if a patient is harmed, and it is unclear whether the FDA, which normally requires approval before software that diagnoses or treats can be sold, will accept the pilots.
summary: Nextgov/FCW reports that Utah announced three new pilots last week in its AI sandbox, the state programme we covered on 6 and 8 Oct 2026 that lets companies test technology under official oversight in return for lighter rules; they cover AI that refills prescriptions for chronic conditions, writes first prescriptions for acne and offers physical therapy online. What is new is that Zach Boyd, director of Utah's Office of Artificial Intelligence Policy, said at the ADAPT conference in Santa Fe, New Mexico, on Thursday 15 Oct 2026 that the state hopes to unveil a liability bill this month or next, and has not yet settled how legal blame should be split between the AI and the clinicians who oversee it.
notes: Continues our Utah coverage: the Nolla Health acne-prescription app (6 Oct 2026 edition) and the six outside evaluators (8 Oct 2026 edition). Nextgov/FCW does not name the pilot companies, so the acne pilot is probably but not certainly Nolla Health. New today: the liability bill timing, the FDA question, the weekly working group with the licensing board and the drugs removed from the refill list. The conference remarks (15 Oct) fall before the 16 Oct window. Tracking code removed from the link.
